To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(i) adjustment may increase or decrease the bias in a parameter, and (ii) in some circumstances, adjustment may introduce bias in a parameter.

the following rules hold for all cases in which the causal effect of X on Y is not confounded by Z: 1. Adjustment for Z will reduce the bias if the effect of X on Z is positive and the effect of Z on Y is negative.

(1) the direction of bias due to adjustment for an intermediate variable can be predicted by a graphical rule that is applicable to any type of dependence (causal or not) and (2) the direction of the bias due to adjustment is opposite that of the bias due the omission of the confounder.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how the causal structure of a system of variables affects the consequences of adjusting for a third, confounding variable.
the consequences of adjusting for a third (or more) variable in a regression model, and how to detect when such an adjustment will alter the degree of association or bias in an effect.
the effects of conditioning on the strength of associations between two variables.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in general, adjusting for a third (or more) variable will alter the association of two variables if the association between the third and one of those two variables depends on the value of the other variable.

adjustment for a variable X will not alter the degree of association (or bias) between Y and Z unless the association between Y and Z depends on the value of X (i.e., unless there is a confounding effect of X on the Y-Z association).

, in a causal context, adjusting for a variable that is not on the path between the exposure and outcome will not affect the bias in the estimate of the causal effect, while adjusting for a variable on the path will affect the bias, sometimes in a way that is predictable, and sometimes unpredictably.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, for the purpose of bias reduction, adjustment can be useful, harmful, or neutral, and that the direction of the bias reduction is determined by whether the adjustment is for the cause, the effect, or a collider.

the direction and magnitude of bias due to adjusting for a third factor depends on the causal graph structure, and the direction and magnitude also depend on the nature of the association between the third factor and the two variables of primary interest.

the graphical rules for detecting noncollapsibility and the graphical rules for identifying situations where the bias in an association is reduced by adjustment are identical, while the graphical rules for situations where the bias is increased by adjustment differ.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the direction in which a dependence changes under adjustment is not necessarily the direction in which an association changes.
the direction of the bias introduced by an adjustment can be predicted from the sign of the association between the exposure and the confounder.
the effects of adjusting for a third covariate on the association of the first with the second can be predicted from the graphical structure of the model.
